items.q: When is the best time to prune trees in southern Ontario?
items.a: For most deciduous trees, the dormant season from late fall through winter, roughly November to March, is the best window. With the leaves down the branch structure is easy to read, most insects and diseases are inactive so there is less infection risk, and the cuts close cleanly as spring growth begins. A few exceptions: maple, birch, walnut, elm and beech ooze sap heavily if cut in late winter or early spring, which looks messy but does not harm the tree. If the bleeding bothers you we can prune those in early summer instead. Oaks are a special case because of oak wilt, so we keep oak pruning to the dormant months and avoid April through October. Dead, broken or diseased wood can come off any time of year, oaks aside. Spring-flowering trees like lilac, magnolia and crabapple are best pruned right after they finish blooming so you do not lose next year's flowers.

items.q: Do I need a permit to prune or remove a tree on my property?
items.a: It depends on your city and usually on the trunk's diameter, so there is no single answer across our service area. Several municipalities here protect private trees once the trunk passes a certain size, and the threshold and process differ from city to city. Routine maintenance, like taking small branches off a healthy tree, is usually exempt, but larger work on a bigger tree can need a permit. We check the rule that applies to your specific property and flag it before we start any work, so you are never caught off guard. If a permit is required we will tell you plainly rather than cutting first and dealing with it later.

items.q: How do I know if a limb is dangerous?
items.a: A few signs are worth taking seriously: a large broken or hanging limb caught up in the canopy (sometimes called a widow-maker), cracks where a branch meets the trunk, a split or crack in the trunk itself, torn or hanging bark, a new or worsening lean, or roots lifting out of the ground. Risk goes up when the limb hangs over something it could damage, like a roof, driveway, walkway or power line. If you can spot any of these from the ground, it is worth a look. Never try to cut a limb that is touching or near a power line, do not climb a damaged tree, and stay clear of branches that are under tension or partly suspended. Call the limb in and we will tell you what we see.

You get a clear, honest quote with no obligation and no high-pressure pitch. Quote visits are free, and most happen within 3 to 5 business days of you reaching out.

items.q: Do you do emergency tree work?
items.a: For an active hazard like a limb on a roof or a vehicle, call and we will tell you honestly how fast we can get there. This is an evenings-and-weekends business, so for a genuinely urgent same-day situation during business hours a full daytime crew may reach you faster, and if so we will tell you who to call. Whatever you do, stay clear of any limb near a power line and do not climb or cut a damaged tree yourself. Report anything touching an electrical line to the utility.
